880:
Appalled describes the feeling you get when something shocks you so deeply — because it seems so wrong, cruel, offensive, or unacceptable — that you can barely believe it is actually happening.

It is not just surprise. It is not just disgust. It is both, fused together with a sense of moral horror — the feeling that something should not be this way, and you are stunned that it is.

When you are appalled, three things are happening at once:

  1. You are shocked — you did not expect this, or you cannot quite process that it is real.
  2. You are deeply disturbed — not just mildly uncomfortable, but genuinely horrified or disgusted.
  3. There is a moral or ethical dimension — what you witnessed or heard feels wrong. It violates your sense of decency, fairness, or humanity.

This combination is what makes "appalled" special. It is not just an emotional reaction — it carries a judgment. When you say you are appalled, you are also saying: this is not okay. This should not be happening.

"Appalled" is a strong word. It sits on the serious end of the emotional scale.

Think of it this way:

  • A little bothered → mildly annoyed
  • More bothered → disturbed or troubled
  • Very bothered + shocked → appalled
  • Extreme end → horrified

When someone says they are appalled, they are not mildly upset. They are expressing that what they saw or heard struck them hard — it left them stunned and deeply unsettled.

That said, in everyday casual speech, people sometimes use "appalled" slightly loosely to mean they are very strongly disapproving of something — even if it is not a life-or-death situation. Context tells you how intense the feeling really is.

You can be appalled by many kinds of things — what they all share is that they seem deeply unacceptable to the person feeling it:

  • Cruelty or violence: Witnessing how an animal is being treated can leave someone appalled.
  • Rudeness or disrespect: A person who is abusive to a waiter might leave onlookers appalled.
  • Injustice: Learning that an innocent person was punished harshly while the guilty went free can be appalling.
  • Shocking incompetence or negligence: A doctor who ignores a patient's obvious symptoms might appal the patient's family.
  • Moral failings: Discovering that someone you trusted behaved dishonestly or hypocritically can leave you appalled.
  • Poor conditions or standards: Visiting a hospital and finding it filthy and neglected can appal a visitor who expects basic standards of care.

Notice that in every case, there is a gap between what should be and what is — and that gap is what produces the feeling of being appalled.

These words are close neighbors, but they are not identical:

Shocked — Pure surprise. Something unexpected happened. There is no strong moral flavor here. You can be shocked by good news too ("I was shocked when I won the prize!"). Appalled always carries a negative, disturbing quality.

Disgusted — The focus is on finding something repulsive, revolting, or deeply unpleasant — often something that feels dirty or offensive to your senses or values. Disgust is one ingredient of being appalled, but appalled is broader — it is also about disbelief and moral horror, not just finding something gross.

Horrified — Very close to appalled. The main difference is that "horrified" leans more toward fear and terror — something frightening. "Appalled" leans more toward moral outrage and stunned disbelief. You might be horrified by a sudden accident; you would more likely be appalled by deliberate cruelty.

Outraged — Outrage is more about anger at an injustice. It is an active, heated emotion — you want to do something about it. Appalled is more of a stunned, sick-in-your-stomach feeling. You can be both at once, but they emphasize different things.

Dismayed — Softer than appalled. Dismay is a sinking sense of disappointment and worry. It does not carry the same shock or moral force that appalled does.

The adjective is almost always followed by "at" or "by" when pointing to the cause, or "to" when followed by a verb:

  • She was appalled by the way he spoke to his elderly mother.
  • The journalist was appalled at the conditions in the refugee camp.
  • He was appalled to learn that the charity had been misusing donations for years.
  • The teacher stood there, appalled, as the students laughed at the bullied child.
  • Visitors to the factory were appalled by what they saw.

You will also often see it strengthened with words like:

  • utterly appalled
  • visibly appalled
  • absolutely appalled
  • deeply appalled

These intensifiers signal that the feeling is at its full force — there is no mild version of being "utterly appalled."
A Picture to Hold In Your Mind

Imagine you are watching a news report. On screen, you see a healthy, well-funded school in one neighbourhood and, right next to it, a crumbling, barely-functioning school in a poorer neighbourhood — same city, same government, wildly different resources. You see children sitting on broken floors with no books.

That sick, stunned, disbelieving feeling — how can this be allowed to happen? This is wrong. This should not exist. — that is being appalled.

If you ever need to quickly recall what "appalled" means:

Appalled = shocked + horrified + moral disbelief, all at once — because something feels deeply, unacceptably wrong.
881:
Appalling means so bad that it causes shock, horror, or disgust. It describes something that doesn't just make you feel unhappy or uncomfortable — it hits you hard. It disturbs you. It makes you feel that what you are seeing, hearing, or experiencing is deeply, seriously wrong or unacceptable.

The key to this word is the reaction it produces. Something appalling doesn't just fall short of expectations — it offends your sense of what is right, decent, or acceptable. It can leave you speechless, sick to your stomach, or filled with outrage.

Imagine you visit a hospital and find that patients are lying on dirty floors, receiving no care, and being treated with cruelty. You would not say the situation is "not great" or "a bit disappointing." You would say it is appalling — because what you are witnessing shocks you at a deep level. It feels wrong. It feels like something that should not exist in a decent world.

That sense of moral shock or horror is at the heart of "appalling." The word carries weight. It signals that something has crossed a line — not just a line of quality or preference, but often a line of human decency.

"Appalling" sits near the top of the scale of "bad." Think of it this way:

Disappointing → Bad → Very bad → Terrible → Appalling

When you call something appalling, you are not mildly criticising it. You are saying it is shockingly, horrifyingly, or disgustingly bad. It is a strong word, and using it tells people that your reaction is intense.
Two Main Ways It Is Used

"Appalling" has two closely related uses. Both share the same core meaning — shockingly bad — but they differ in how serious or heavy the context is.

1. Moral Horror (The Stronger Use)

This is where "appalling" carries its full emotional weight. It describes situations involving cruelty, suffering, injustice, or behaviour that shocks your conscience.

  • "The treatment of workers in that factory was appalling — they worked 16-hour shifts for almost no pay in dangerous conditions."
  • "The violence carried out against civilians during the war was appalling."
  • "It is appalling that children in some parts of the world have no access to clean drinking water."

In these cases, the word signals moral outrage. You are not just saying something is bad in quality — you are saying it is wrong, and that it deeply disturbs you.

2. Very Poor Quality (The Everyday Use)

"Appalling" can also be used in more ordinary, everyday situations to describe something of very low quality or standard. Here, the moral horror is reduced, but the sense of strong disapproval remains. This use is sometimes slightly exaggerated for emphasis — a way of stressing just how bad something is.

  • "The food at that restaurant was appalling — it was cold, tasteless, and badly cooked."
  • "His punctuation is appalling; he puts commas in the most random places."
  • "The weather during our holiday was appalling — it rained every single day."

In these examples, no one has necessarily committed a moral wrong. The word is being used to convey strong dissatisfaction or a very low standard.
How to Tell Which Use Is Intended

Context does all the work here. When "appalling" is used to describe human behaviour, injustice, suffering, or cruelty, it carries serious moral weight. When it is used to describe food, weather, handwriting, or a sports performance, it is the everyday, emphatic version. Both uses are correct and common.

Certain words pair naturally with "appalling" in everyday English. Knowing these combinations helps you recognise and use the word more fluently.

  • Appalling conditions — extremely bad living or working conditions
  • Appalling behaviour — conduct that shocks or disgusts
  • Appalling treatment — the way someone is treated in a horrifying way
  • Appalling state — something in a terrible, shocking condition (e.g., "The building was in an appalling state.")
  • Appalling violence / cruelty — violence or cruelty that causes horror
  • Appalling weather — weather that is very bad (everyday use)

You will also often see intensifiers placed before "appalling" to make it even stronger:

  • "Simply appalling."
  • "Truly appalling."
  • "Absolutely appalling."
  • "Nothing short of appalling."

These additions signal that the speaker is deeply affected and wants to leave no doubt about how strongly they feel.

Understanding what a word does not mean is just as important as understanding what it does mean.

It is not a mild word. You would not use "appalling" for something that is merely a little inconvenient, slightly boring, or a minor letdown. If a film is just not very interesting, it might be "dull" or "disappointing" — not appalling. Reserve "appalling" for things that genuinely shock or strongly disgust you (or that are so bad they demand a strong word).

It is not the same as "surprising." Something can surprise you without being appalling. Appalling always carries a negative charge. You cannot say something is "appallingly good" — the word only moves in one direction: toward the bad, the shocking, and the unacceptable. (Note: "appallingly" as an adverb can be used sarcastically — e.g., "appallingly good luck" — but the adjective "appalling" itself is always negative.)

It is not purely about appearance. Something appalling may or may not look ugly. The word is about the reaction it triggers — the shock, the outrage, the disgust — not just its visual qualities.

"Appalling" is a standard English word. It is not slang, not overly formal, and not outdated. You will encounter it comfortably in:

  • Newspaper articles and news reports
  • Formal speeches and official statements
  • Everyday conversation
  • Written essays and literature

It is the kind of word that a judge, a journalist, a teacher, and a friend at the dinner table could all use naturally, each in their own context.
A Final Way to Remember It

If you want a mental anchor for this word, think of it this way:

Appalling = so bad it appals you — it stops you in your tracks, makes your stomach turn, and makes you feel that what you are witnessing or experiencing is deeply, seriously wrong or unacceptably poor.

Whether it is the appalling cruelty of an injustice or the appalling quality of a cold, overpriced meal, the word always tells you: this is not just bad — this is shockingly, unacceptably bad.
882: Quick note on spelling: The correct spelling is appallingly — double p, double l. This is worth memorising right away.

Appallingly means "in a way that causes shock, horror, or deep disgust" — or, when used as an intensifier, "to an extremely bad and disturbing degree."

It is the adverb form of the adjective appalling, which itself comes from the verb appall — meaning to fill someone with horror or dismay.

Think of it this way: if something is merely bad, you might frown. If something is appallingly bad, your jaw drops. Your stomach turns. You feel a mix of disbelief and moral outrage that something this bad is even possible.

Appallingly does two jobs in English, and understanding both will make you a confident user of this word.

1. As a Manner Adverb — describing how something happens

Here, it tells you the way in which an action is done — specifically, in a way that is deeply shocking or horrifying.

  • The refugees were treated appallingly.
  • He behaved appallingly at his own wedding.
  • The workers were paid appallingly.

In each of these, the word answers the question "How?" — and the answer is: in a way that should fill any decent person with horror.

2. As an Intensifier — making an adjective or adverb stronger

Here, appallingly sits in front of another descriptive word and amplifies it. It means something close to "shockingly" or "to an extremely bad degree."

  • The hospital was appallingly understaffed.
  • She was appallingly rude to the waiter.
  • The instructions were appallingly unclear.
  • He arrived appallingly late.

In these cases, it is not just saying "very" — it is saying "so bad that it should shock you."
The Emotional Weight That Sets It Apart

This is the part most learners miss, and it is the most important thing to truly understand this word.

Appallingly is not just a synonym for "very badly." It always carries the speaker's strong emotional reaction — a sense of moral outrage, disbelief, or revulsion. When you use this word, you are not just describing a situation; you are making a judgment that the situation is far below any acceptable standard.

Compare these sentences:

  • The roads are badly maintained. → Simple fact, neutral tone.
  • The roads are appallingly maintained. → The speaker is horrified. They feel this is a disgrace. They want you to feel that too.

Or:

  • He was very rude. → Factual observation.
  • He was appallingly rude. → The rudeness was so extreme it caused genuine shock and disgust.

This emotional charge is always present. Even when used in casual or slightly exaggerated speech — "The weather has been appallingly cold this week" — the word borrows its power from that core sense of shocking, intolerable badness.
How It Compares to Similar Words

English has many words that mean "very badly" or "shockingly." Here is how appallingly stands apart:

  • Terribly / Awfully / Dreadfully — These mean "very" or "to a bad degree," but they have largely lost their original emotional force in everyday speech. Saying "I'm terribly sorry" feels routine. Saying "I'm appallingly sorry" would actually sound strange — because appallingly still carries real shock value.
  • Shockingly — This focuses on the surprise of something. Appallingly focuses on both the shock and the horror or moral wrongness.
  • Disgracefully — This focuses specifically on shame and dishonour. Appallingly is broader — it covers anything that causes horror, not just things that are shameful.

Appallingly sits at the strong end of the scale. It is a word with weight and feeling, and native speakers notice when it is used.
The Kinds of Situations Where It Fits Naturally

Appallingly tends to appear in situations involving:

  • Human suffering or neglect: The prisoners were appallingly malnourished.
  • Moral failures: The company behaved appallingly toward its employees.
  • Incompetence or negligence: The project was appallingly managed.
  • Extreme rudeness or cruelty: He spoke appallingly to his own mother.
  • Standards that fall far below expectations: The service at that hospital was appallingly slow.

It is less commonly used to describe trivial things, though in casual, exaggerated speech it does appear — "This coffee is appallingly bitter" — but even then, it borrows its power from its stronger meaning.

Because appallingly sounds so strong and dramatic, do not overuse it. If you describe everything as appalling, the word loses its impact. Reserve it for situations where the badness is genuinely extreme, deeply upsetting, or far below what any reasonable person would accept. That is when the word earns its place — and earns the reader's or listener's full attention.

Appallingly means: in a way that is shockingly, horrifyingly, or disgracefully bad — far beyond what is tolerable or acceptable. It always carries the speaker's strong emotional disapproval. It can describe how something is done (manner) or how extreme something bad is (intensifier). It is stronger, more charged, and more emotionally loaded than everyday words like terribly or very badly.

Master this word and you have not just learned a vocabulary item — you have learned a tool for expressing genuine moral and emotional reaction with precision.
883:
Apparatus means a collection of parts, tools, instruments, or components that work together as a unified whole to perform a specific function. The single most important thing to understand about this word is that it almost always implies a system — not just one thing in isolation, but multiple parts that connect and cooperate to achieve something.

Think of it this way: a single screw is not an apparatus. But an oxygen mask connected to a tank, with tubes and valves and a harness, all working together so a firefighter can breathe in a burning building — that entire setup is a breathing apparatus.

1. A physical set of equipment or machinery

This is the most direct and common meaning. When used in this sense, apparatus refers to a group of physical instruments, devices, or tools that are assembled together and function as one system.

A laboratory apparatus, for example, is the whole collection of flasks, tubes, clamps, burners, and stands a scientist uses together in an experiment. A gym might have exercise apparatus — the various machines and equipment that together make up a workout setup. A rescue team might use breathing apparatus — the complete gear allowing someone to breathe in a dangerous environment.

What separates the word apparatus from a simpler word like tool or device is that it suggests something more elaborate — a complete, coordinated system rather than a single, standalone object.

2. A large, complex system of people and structures (especially in politics and government)

This is a very widely used meaning, especially in journalism, politics, and academic writing. Here, "apparatus" refers to the entire machinery of an organization — not physical machines, but the whole network of people, rules, departments, and processes that work together to keep a large institution running.

For example, "the state apparatus" means the entire machinery of a government — its courts, police, military, civil servants, regulations, and all the structures that allow the state to function and exercise power. "The party apparatus" means the internal organizational machine of a political party — its officials, offices, procedures, and networks. "The propaganda apparatus" means the complete system used to produce and spread propaganda — the writers, broadcasters, publishers, censors, and channels all working in coordination.

In this sense, calling something an "apparatus" often carries a slightly cold or mechanical feeling — it describes a large, often impersonal system that operates with the relentlessness of a machine. When a journalist says "the security apparatus," they're not just talking about a few police officers; they're pointing to the entire, interconnected infrastructure of surveillance, intelligence agencies, and enforcement working as one system.

3. A group of organs in the body (biological/anatomical use)

In science — particularly biology and anatomy — apparatus describes a group of organs or body structures that work together to carry out a particular function inside a living body.

The digestive apparatus, for instance, includes the mouth, esophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas, and all related organs — everything that cooperates to break down food and absorb nutrients. The vocal apparatus includes the lungs, larynx, vocal cords, tongue, lips, and teeth — all the parts that work together to produce speech. Inside cells, the Golgi apparatus is a specific structure responsible for packaging and distributing proteins.
A Less Common but Important Meaning: Critical Apparatus

In academic scholarship and publishing, a "critical apparatus" (or simply "apparatus") is the body of supplementary material that scholars attach to a text to help readers understand it deeply. This includes footnotes, commentary, notes on different versions of the text, and references to sources.

For example, a scholarly edition of an ancient poem might have a critical apparatus listing every place where historians disagree about the exact original wording, and explaining the evidence for each possibility. You are most likely to encounter this meaning in academic or literary contexts.

Across all its meanings — physical equipment, political systems, biological organs, and scholarly material — the word apparatus always carries the same underlying idea: a complex, coordinated system made of multiple parts that work together toward a single purpose. It always implies organization, interconnection, and function.

The plural is most commonly apparatuses in everyday English. However, "apparatus" itself is also accepted as a plural (especially in scientific and formal writing), where you might read "various apparatus were used in the experiment." You may occasionally see "apparati," but this is generally considered incorrect and is best avoided.
Tone and Register: When Do People Use This Word?

"Apparatus" is a formal word. In casual conversation, people are far more likely to say "equipment," "setup," "gear," "system," or "machine." You will most commonly encounter "apparatus" in scientific writing, academic texts, journalism about politics or government, legal language, and formal descriptions of technology or biology.

When someone chooses the word "apparatus" over a simpler alternative, they are often deliberately emphasizing the complexity, the systematized nature, and the coordinated functioning of whatever they are describing. It gives a sense of scale and structure that words like "tool" or "device" don't carry.

"Apparatus" (noun) = a complex, organized system of parts working together for a purpose. It can mean physical equipment, a large human organization (especially political), or a group of body organs — but in every case, the emphasis is on a system that functions as a whole, not any single isolated part.
884: "Apparent" is one of the most interesting adjectives in English, because it carries two meanings that seem to pull in opposite directions — yet both are correct, and both are widely used. Mastering this word means understanding both meanings and knowing which one a speaker or writer intends in a given situation.

Meaning 1: Clearly visible, obvious, or easy to understand.

When something is "apparent," it can mean that it is plain for anyone to see — there is no doubt about it, no effort needed to notice it. It sits right in front of you, undeniable.

The damage to the car was apparent. — You could see it clearly. No one needed to point it out.

Her excitement was apparent the moment she walked in. — Anyone in the room could tell she was excited, without being told.

In this sense, "apparent" is very close in meaning to words like obvious, evident, and plain.

Meaning 2: Seeming to be true, but not necessarily true.

Here is where the word gets genuinely interesting. "Apparent" can also describe something that looks a certain way on the surface, but which may not actually be that way underneath. It is the appearance of something — the impression it gives — without a guarantee that the impression is accurate.

The apparent cause of the fire was a short circuit. — Based on the evidence available, it seemed like a short circuit caused the fire. But investigators aren't completely certain; that is simply what it looks like so far.

Her apparent confidence surprised her colleagues. — She seemed confident. But she might have been terrified inside. The confidence was the outward impression she gave, not a confirmed inner truth.

In this sense, "apparent" is close in meaning to words like seeming, supposed, and ostensible.
Why Do These Two Meanings Coexist — And How Do You Tell Them Apart?

This is the part that confuses most learners, and it deserves a careful explanation.

Both meanings actually grow from the same root idea: how something appears to the eye or the mind. If something appears very clearly and undeniably, you get Meaning 1 (obvious). If something merely appears to be a certain way without you being sure it truly is, you get Meaning 2 (seeming but uncertain).

The key is context and tone. Ask yourself: is the writer saying something is beyond doubt, or is the writer deliberately leaving room for doubt?

Consider these two sentences side by side:

"The pain was apparent on his face." — Here, the pain was visible and obvious to all. Meaning 1.

"He showed apparent pain, but the doctors were skeptical." — Here, he seemed to be in pain, but the doctors didn't entirely believe it. Meaning 2.

Notice how in the second sentence, there is a hint of skepticism or uncertainty. That is almost always the signal that Meaning 2 is at play. Whenever "apparent" is used to subtly question whether something is really what it looks like, you are dealing with Meaning 2.
A Crucial Nuance: "Apparent" Can Be a Polite Form of Doubt

In formal or careful writing — journalism, academic papers, legal language — "apparent" is very often used deliberately to avoid stating something as a confirmed fact. It is a way of saying this is what it looks like, but we are not yet certain.

The apparent winner of the election is Senator Mills. — Votes are still being counted; she seems to have won, but it is not yet official.

Police are investigating the apparent murder. — It looks like a murder, but the investigation is ongoing.

This is not vagueness for its own sake. It is precise, responsible language. Using "apparent" in this way protects writers from stating something as fact before it is confirmed.

"For no apparent reason" — This means something happened without any visible or obvious cause. She started crying for no apparent reason. Nobody watching could figure out why.

"It is apparent that..." — This is a formal way of saying "it is clear that" or "it is obvious that." It is apparent that more funding is needed. This uses Meaning 1.

"Heir apparent" — This is a fixed phrase meaning the person who is expected to inherit a position, title, or role — especially a throne. The heir apparent to the company's leadership is the founder's daughter. This uses Meaning 2 in a sense: the person is the presumed and expected successor, though the formal transfer has not yet happened.

The adverb form, "apparently," works in exactly the same way and carries the same two flavors of meaning, but it comes up even more often in everyday speech.

When it means "clearly / obviously": Apparently, she had not slept in days — her eyes were red and exhausted. It was evident.

When it means "it seems / I've heard / supposedly": Apparently, the restaurant is closed on Mondays. — You were told this, or you read it somewhere, but you haven't confirmed it yourself. There is a degree of uncertainty.

In everyday spoken English, "apparently" very frequently signals that you are reporting something you heard secondhand, or something that surprised you. Apparently, they're getting divorced. — You heard this; you can't fully verify it.
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

If you had to carry just one idea away from this explanation, let it be this:

"Apparent" lives in the space between appearance and reality. Sometimes that gap is zero — the thing appears true and is true, plain for all to see (Meaning 1). Sometimes that gap is unknown or suspicious — the thing appears true, but you're not sure it actually is (Meaning 2). The word is always about how something presents itself to the observer, and whether that presentation can be fully trusted depends on the context.

Once you see "apparent" this way — as a word fundamentally about the relationship between surface and truth — both meanings will feel like two sides of the same coin, and you will never confuse them again.
885: Apparently signals that something seems to be true, but the speaker is not stating it as a definite fact. It creates a gap between "what appears to be" and "what definitely is." The speaker is stepping back slightly from a claim, rather than owning it fully.

1. Based on what you can observe (appearances)

You use "apparently" when something looks a certain way from the outside, but you're not fully sure it really is that way.

  • "She was apparently fine after the fall."
    → From what I could see, she seemed fine — but I can't be certain what she was feeling inside.
  • "The building is apparently abandoned."
    → It looks abandoned based on what I can observe, but I haven't confirmed it.

The key feeling here is: "This is what it looks like, but I could be wrong."

2. Based on what you heard or were told (hearsay)

This is the most common everyday use. You use "apparently" when you're passing on information that you didn't personally witness or verify — you heard it, read it, or someone told you.

  • "Apparently, the train is delayed."
    → I heard/read that the train is delayed. I'm not at the station myself — I'm relaying what I was told.
  • "Apparently, he used to be an actor."
    → Someone told me this, or I read it somewhere. I didn't witness it myself.

This use is socially very useful: it politely signals, "I'm sharing this information, but I can't personally guarantee it." It's honest. It lets you share something without pretending you know more than you do.
The tonal layer: surprise and skepticism

"Apparently" can also carry a faint feeling of surprise, irony, or even mild disbelief — especially in speech.

  • "Apparently, we all have to work this weekend."
    → Said with mild surprise or annoyance. The speaker didn't expect this.
  • "He's apparently some kind of genius."
    → Said with a hint of skepticism. The speaker is quoting what others say, but might not fully believe it.

In these cases, "apparently" quietly signals: "This is what I've been told — though I'm a little surprised, or not entirely convinced."
Where in a sentence can it go?

"Apparently" can appear in three positions, all grammatically correct:

  • Beginning: "Apparently, she didn't get the message." → Most common in speech.
  • Middle: "She apparently didn't get the message." → Neutral and clean.
  • End: "She didn't get the message, apparently." → Most casual; often carries a slight tone of surprise or dry humor.

Understanding "apparently" becomes sharper when you see how it differs from words that look similar.

Obviously / Clearly
These mean the speaker is completely certain, and the evidence is plain for anyone to see.

  • "Obviously, he's upset." → No doubt at all. It's fully clear.
  • "Apparently, he's upset." → Based on how he looks or what someone said. Less certain.

Supposedly
This carries more skepticism than "apparently." It often hints that the speaker doesn't quite believe the claim.

  • "He's supposedly an expert." → I've been told this, but I'm doubtful.
  • "He's apparently an expert." → I've been told or it seems so — neutral, no strong doubt implied.

"Apparently" is more neutral. "Supposedly" often has a skeptical or even mocking edge.

Seemingly
Very similar to "apparently" in the first sense (based on appearances), but slightly more formal, and not used for hearsay.

  • "She was seemingly calm." → Based on appearances.
  • You would not say "Seemingly, the train is delayed" the way you'd say "Apparently, the train is delayed."

Evidently
Similar to "apparently," but slightly more formal and often implies that there is actual visible evidence.

  • "He had evidently been crying." → The evidence (red eyes, tears) makes it clear.
One critical warning: "apparently" does NOT mean "obviously"

Because the word looks like it comes from "apparent" — and "apparent" can sometimes mean "obvious" in formal writing — people sometimes mistakenly use "apparently" to mean "clearly" or "obviously." In modern everyday English, this is wrong.

Modern "apparently" almost always signals uncertainty or hearsay, not certainty. If you want to say something is completely clear and beyond doubt, use "clearly," "obviously," or "evidently" — not "apparently."

Whenever you're unsure whether "apparently" fits, try replacing it with one of these phrases:

  • "It seems that..."
  • "From what I can see..."
  • "I heard that..."
  • "According to what I was told..."

If any of these fits naturally in your sentence, "apparently" is the right word.
"Apparently" = This is what it seems like, or this is what I've heard — but I'm not stating it as my own certain fact.
886:
An apparition is a ghostly figure or image that appears suddenly — something seen that feels unreal, supernatural, or deeply unsettling. Think of it as the visual experience of seeing something (usually a person or figure) that should not be there, or that cannot quite be explained.

The most natural synonym is a ghost — but "apparition" is a richer, more precise word. Here's why: a ghost is what the thing is; an apparition is the experience of seeing it. It puts emphasis on the moment of appearance itself — the sudden, startling act of something materializing before your eyes.

1. A Ghost or Supernatural Figure

This is the most common meaning. An apparition is a spirit, phantom, or ghostly form — usually of a dead person — that becomes visible to the living. It is not a solid, physical body. It seems to float, glow, fade, or pass through walls. It appears without warning and often vanishes just as suddenly.

"The old woman swore she saw an apparition at the foot of her bed — the pale, translucent figure of her late husband, staring at her in silence before dissolving into the darkness."

Key qualities of an apparition in this sense:

  • It looks like a person (or sometimes an animal), but is not physically there
  • It is seen rather than touched or heard
  • It appears and disappears mysteriously
  • It causes shock, fear, or awe in whoever witnesses it
  • It may or may not be real — the word leaves that deliberately open

2. The Act of Something Appearing Suddenly and Strikingly

In a broader sense, an apparition can refer to the sudden, unexpected appearance of anything — not just a ghost — when that appearance feels dramatic, dreamlike, or hard to believe. This usage is more literary and figurative.

"Out of the thick fog, the apparition of a great ship slowly emerged — silent and enormous — before disappearing back into the mist."

"She walked into the room like an apparition — so pale, so still, so unexpected — that everyone fell silent."

Here, the word is not claiming something is supernatural. It is saying that the manner of appearing was so sudden, so striking, and so strange that it felt ghostly or unreal.
What Makes "Apparition" Special — The Feeling It Carries

This is where the word truly comes alive. "Apparition" is not a neutral word. It carries a specific atmosphere with it:

  • Mystery — you're not sure what you saw
  • Eeriness — it makes the hair on the back of your neck stand up
  • Fragility — it can vanish at any moment
  • Unreality — it exists on the edge between what is real and what is imagined

When a writer chooses "apparition" over "ghost" or "figure," they are doing so deliberately — to wrap the moment in uncertainty and unease. An apparition is not something you can grab or prove. It is something witnessed, something that leaves you shaken and questioning your own senses.

These words are close cousins, but each has its own flavor:

Ghost — the most everyday word for a spirit of the dead. Casual and straightforward. "I believe in ghosts."

Apparition — emphasizes the visual appearance of the ghost; more dramatic, more literary, more unsettling. "An apparition materialized before him."

Phantom — stresses that something is an illusion, not truly real. A phantom is something deceptive. "The phantom ship lured sailors to their doom."

Specter (or Spectre) — a ghost with a strong sense of threat or dread looming over it. "The specter of death."

Vision — something seen, often beautiful, prophetic, or holy — not necessarily frightening. "She had a vision of angels."

Hallucination — something seen that is definitively not real, produced entirely by the mind, usually due to illness, drugs, or extreme exhaustion. A hallucination is inside your head. An apparition might be real — that ambiguity is the whole point.
A Special Real-World Context: Religious Apparitions

The word "apparition" is also used seriously in religious contexts. Across many traditions, people have reported seeing sacred figures — such as the Virgin Mary or various saints — appear to them in moments of deep spiritual significance. These are called apparitions, and they are treated with great reverence. The most famous examples include the Marian apparitions (appearances of the Virgin Mary) reported at Lourdes in France and Fátima in Portugal. This use of the word is not considered fiction or superstition by those who believe — it is a sincere, solemn report of something witnessed.

An apparition is:

  1. A ghost or supernatural figure that appears suddenly and visibly — the experience of seeing a spirit
  2. The sudden, striking, dreamlike appearance of anything that feels unreal or hard to believe
  3. A word that carries mood — mystery, eeriness, fragility, and the blurring of reality and imagination

It is a word that lives in the space between seeing and believing, between the real world and whatever lies beyond it. When you use or read the word "apparition," know that something extraordinary — or at least something that feels extraordinary — has just appeared before someone's eyes.
887: To appeal means to reach out — either because something pulls you toward it, or because you are reaching out to someone for help or intervention. This "reaching" quality runs through all its meanings.
Meaning 1: To attract or interest someone

When something appeals to you, it means it attracts you, interests you, or pleases you in some way. You feel drawn to it.

Structure: something + appeals to + someone

"The idea of living abroad really appeals to me." → It attracts me; I find it interesting.

"Spicy food doesn't appeal to everyone." → Not everyone likes it.

"Her sense of humor appealed to him immediately." → It attracted him; he found it charming.

Important: Notice that the thing doing the attracting is always the subject. The person who feels attracted comes after "to." So you'd say "This plan appeals to me," not "I appeal to this plan" (that would mean something very different — see Meaning 2).

A subtle but important point: When something appeals to you, it doesn't necessarily mean you love it deeply. It simply means you find it interesting, pleasant, or worth considering. "This option appeals to me" is softer than "I love this option" — it says the option feels right or attractive to you, without strong emotion.
Meaning 2: To make an earnest, heartfelt request

When you appeal to someone, you are making a serious, sincere request — often directed at their emotions, sense of justice, authority, or compassion. This is not casual asking. It carries urgency, sincerity, or desperation.

Structure: someone + appeals to + someone + (to do something / for something)

"The leader appealed to the crowd to remain calm." → He sincerely urged them; he reached out to their sense of reason.

"She appealed to her professor for more time." → She made a sincere, earnest request.

"He appealed to her kindness." → He invoked her kindness; he asked her to act based on it.

You can also appeal for something directly:

"The organization appealed for donations." → They made a public, serious request for donations.

"The survivors appealed for help." → They urgently requested help.

Key nuance: To appeal to someone's something (kindness, reason, conscience, better nature) means you are deliberately invoking that quality in them — you are saying, in effect, "I know you have this quality in you; please let it guide you now."

"She appealed to his sense of fairness to reconsider the decision."

This is a powerful, almost rhetorical act. You are not just asking — you are reminding someone of who they are or what they stand for.
Meaning 3 (Legal): To formally challenge a decision

In legal contexts, to appeal means to formally ask a higher court or authority to review and overturn a decision made by a lower court or body. When you disagree with a ruling and believe it was wrong, you appeal — you take the matter to a higher level of authority.

Structure: appeal (a decision) / appeal against (a decision)

"The defendant decided to appeal the verdict." → He formally challenged the court's decision by taking it to a higher court.

"The company appealed against the ruling." → (British English) They formally objected and requested a review.

"She lost the case at the lower court, but she can still appeal." → She can take the matter higher.

A clear way to picture this: Imagine a ladder of courts. You lost on a lower rung. When you appeal, you climb to the next rung and say, "This decision was wrong. I want a higher authority to look at this again."

Note: You can simply say "she appealed" without naming the decision, and it still means she formally challenged the outcome.
How to tell which meaning is being used

Look at who or what the subject is, and the context:

  • If a thing (a plan, a book, an idea, food) is doing something to a person → Meaning 1 (attraction). "This career path appeals to me."
  • If a person is urgently or sincerely asking someone else → Meaning 2 (earnest request). "He appealed to the public for support."
  • If the context involves courts, verdicts, rulings, or judges → Meaning 3 (legal challenge). "They appealed the decision."

The preposition you use with "appeal" matters greatly:

  • appeal to someone — used in all three meanings (depends entirely on context)
  • appeal for something — used in Meaning 2 (appeal for calm, appeal for funds)
  • appeal against something — used in Meaning 3, especially in British English (appeal against a sentence)

In American English, the legal sense often drops "against":

"She appealed the ruling." (American) vs. "She appealed against the ruling." (British)
One word, three very different actions

To bring it all together:

When a thing appeals to you, it means you are attracted to it — you like or find it interesting.

When a person appeals to another person, it means they are making a serious, sincere request — often invoking that person's compassion, reason, or authority.

When someone appeals a decision, it means they are formally challenging it before a higher authority — saying the decision was wrong and must be reviewed.

The word is always about reaching — toward something attractive, toward someone's help, or toward a higher authority for justice.
888:
When something is appealing, it has a quality that attracts you toward it — it draws your attention, interest, or desire. It makes you think "I like this," "I want this," or "This is good."

Think of it this way: imagine you walk past a bakery and see a perfectly made cake in the window. It looks so good that you stop and stare. That cake is appealing. Now imagine a job offer that comes with great pay, good hours, and interesting work. That offer is also appealing. Now imagine a friendly, warm person who makes everyone feel comfortable. That person is appealing too.

So "appealing" is a broad, flexible word. It covers anything — a person, an object, an idea, a design, an offer, a story — that has a positive, attractive quality that draws people in.
What Exactly Does It Mean to Be "Appealing"?

Something appealing has one or more of these qualities that make it attractive:

1. It looks good (visually appealing)
A colour combination, a room's decoration, a dish of food, a piece of clothing — when these look pleasant and attractive to the eye, they are appealing.

"The restaurant had a very appealing interior — warm lights, wooden tables, and soft music."

2. It sounds good or feels like a good idea (intellectually or emotionally appealing)
An idea, a plan, an offer, or a suggestion can be appealing when it sounds attractive and worth pursuing.

"Working from home sounded very appealing to her after years of long commutes."
"The professor made an appealing argument that was hard to disagree with."

3. A person has a charm or warmth about them
When a person is described as appealing, it usually means they have a likable, charming, or attractive quality — not necessarily physical beauty alone, but a overall pleasant, magnetic presence.

"He had an appealing personality — cheerful, honest, and always ready to help."
"The child had an appealing smile that made everyone in the room feel warm."

4. Something tempts or invites you
Food, an activity, a destination — when something makes you feel like you want to go for it, try it, or have it, it is appealing.

"A quiet holiday in the mountains sounded very appealing after a stressful month."
"The menu had several appealing options, and she had a hard time choosing."

The key feeling behind this word is being drawn toward something. It is a positive pull. Something appealing doesn't push you away — it pulls you in. It makes you lean forward, not step back.

This pull can be:

  • To the eyes → it looks beautiful or pleasant
  • To the mind → it sounds smart, logical, or interesting
  • To the heart → it feels warm, kind, or emotionally touching
  • To your desires → you want it, crave it, or wish for it

"Appealing" sits in the middle range of attractiveness words. It is not the strongest word you could use, but it is genuine and meaningful.

Think of it like this scale:

Slightly positive → Pleasant → Appealing → Attractive → Stunning / Gorgeous

So when you call something "appealing," you're saying it is clearly and genuinely attractive — but you're not necessarily saying it is the most beautiful or incredible thing you've ever seen. It's a grounded, honest compliment.

These words are close in meaning, but each has its own shade:

  • Attractive — Similar to appealing, but slightly more focused on looks or physical qualities. "Appealing" feels warmer and broader.
  • Charming — More about personality, social grace, or a certain magical quality in a person or place.
  • Enticing / Tempting — Stronger pull toward desire. These words carry a sense of almost irresistible attraction, often toward food, pleasure, or something you're slightly unsure about.
  • Inviting — Suggests warmth and comfort; makes you feel welcome (an inviting room, an inviting atmosphere).
  • Pleasing — Gives you a sense of satisfaction and happiness; often used for things that are pleasant to look at or hear.

"Appealing" can often replace any of these in a sentence because it is versatile. But each of the above carries its own specific flavour that "appealing" doesn't always match exactly.

To understand a word fully, it helps to know what its opposite looks like.

Something that is unappealing (the direct opposite) fails to attract you — or actively puts you off. A messy, dirty plate of food looks unappealing. A boring, repetitive job is unappealing. A rude, cold person is unappealing.

Other opposites: off-putting (it actually repels you), uninviting (it doesn't welcome you), repulsive (it disgust you strongly), disagreeable (it feels unpleasant).

Here are the most natural patterns you'll encounter:

"find something appealing"

"I find minimalist design very appealing."
"She didn't find the offer particularly appealing."

"visually appealing"

"The packaging was visually appealing — clean, colourful, and modern."

"highly appealing"

"The idea of a four-day workweek is highly appealing to most employees."

"less/more appealing"

"The idea of cooking dinner became less appealing after a twelve-hour shift."

"appealing [noun]" (adjective before a noun)

"It was an appealing offer." / "She had an appealing personality." / "An appealing colour scheme."

"sound/look/seem appealing"

"That plan sounds appealing — let's give it a try."
"The dish didn't look very appealing, but it tasted wonderful."

SituationExample

Food: "The freshly baked bread smelled appealing from across the street."

Work: "The job had an appealing mix of creativity and structure."

Travel: "Spending a week in a quiet village with no Wi-Fi sounded oddly appealing."

Design: "The website had a clean, appealing layout that was easy to navigate."

Person: "What made her appealing as a leader was her calm and fairness."

Idea: "His suggestion was appealing because it solved the problem without costing much."

Story/Art: "The novel's main character was deeply appealing — flawed, funny, and honest."

Appealing means attractively good in a way that draws you toward it.

It can describe how something looks, sounds, feels, or comes across. It applies to people, things, ideas, offers, designs, food, places — almost anything. It tells you: this has a quality that makes people like it, want it, or feel drawn to it.

Whenever you see or hear "appealing," ask yourself: what is it about this thing that is attracting the person? The answer — whether it's beauty, warmth, logic, comfort, or desire — is exactly what "appealing" is pointing to.
889: Appear carries one underlying idea: something comes into awareness — whether it physically comes into view, shows up in a place, gives off an impression, or comes out into the world. All the meanings of this word are connected by this sense of arrival or emergence.
Meaning 1: To Come into Sight (Become Visible)

This is the most physical, concrete meaning. Something "appears" when it becomes visible — it was not seen before, and now it is. The focus is on the moment of becoming visible, not on the ongoing state of being visible.

  • "A deer appeared from behind the trees."
  • "Dark clouds appeared on the horizon."
  • "Stars appear as soon as the sun sets."

Notice what makes this meaning work: there is a before (not visible) and an after (visible). If someone is already standing in front of you and you describe what they look like, you wouldn't use this sense of "appear." But if they suddenly walk in, they appear.
Meaning 2: To Seem, or to Give an Impression

This is arguably the most common use of "appear" in everyday English. When something "appears" a certain way, it gives the impression of being that way — based on what you can observe from the outside.

  • "She appeared calm, but inside she was terrified."
  • "The house appeared to be empty."
  • "He appeared tired after the long journey."
  • "It appears that no one informed him about the change."

The most important nuance here: "appear" signals that you are describing an impression or observation, not a confirmed fact. There is always a slight gap between appearance and reality. This is why "appear" is used in careful, precise, or formal writing — it honestly acknowledges that things might not be what they look like.

Compare:

  • "She is exhausted." — This is a statement of fact.
  • "She appears exhausted." — This is what you observe; the reality could be different.

This distinction matters in situations where you want to be accurate and not overstate what you know. A doctor might say, "The patient appears to be in pain," rather than stating it as absolute fact. A journalist might write, "It appears that a mistake was made," rather than asserting it outright.
Meaning 3: To Show Up or Present Yourself Formally

When a person "appears" somewhere in this sense, they arrive and present themselves — often in an official, expected, or significant context.

  • "The witness appeared in court."
  • "She appeared before the committee to answer questions."
  • "The manager appeared at the conference room at exactly noon."

This meaning carries a slightly formal or official flavor. You can use it for casual situations too ("He appeared at my door unexpectedly"), but it often implies that the person's presence carries some weight or was awaited.
Meaning 4: To Be Published or Released

When writing, news, a book, a film, or any piece of media "appears," it becomes available or is released to the public for the first time.

  • "Her debut novel appeared in 2019."
  • "The article appeared on the front page of the newspaper."
  • "A correction appeared in the following week's edition."
  • "The documentary appeared on streaming platforms last month."

This is the word "appear" applied to things — as opposed to people. When a piece of work "appears," it emerges into the world, just like a person appearing in a room.
Meaning 5: To Perform or Be Featured Publicly

When an actor, musician, public figure, or speaker "appears" somewhere, they are featured, perform, or take part in a public event or production.

  • "She appeared in three films that year."
  • "The president appeared on national television."
  • "He appeared as a guest on the podcast."
  • "The band appeared at the music festival for the first time."

This meaning overlaps with Meaning 3 (showing up), but it specifically implies some kind of public role, performance, or feature.

Appear vs. Seem

Both words mean "to give an impression," and in most sentences, they are nearly interchangeable. The subtle difference is:

  • "Seem" tends to express what you personally feel or perceive — it is more internal.
  • "Appear" tends to express what is observable to anyone looking — it is more external and objective.

Compare:

  • "She seems upset." — You personally sense something is off; it's your inner reading.
  • "She appears upset." — Anyone watching would notice it; it is outwardly visible.

In practice, this line blurs frequently. But "appear" is slightly more formal and slightly more objective than "seem."

Appear vs. Look

"Look" is specifically about visual appearance — what your eyes see.

"Appear" is broader — it can cover the whole impression a person or thing creates, including their behavior, tone, circumstances, and context — not just how they look visually.

  • "He looks tired." — His face, eyes, and posture are showing tiredness.
  • "He appears tired." — The overall impression — including how he speaks, moves, and acts — suggests tiredness.

Understanding grammar patterns will help you use the word correctly in your own writing and speaking.

Pattern 1: appear + adjective
"The room appeared clean." / "She appeared nervous."

Pattern 2: appear + to + verb (infinitive)
"He appeared to be sleeping." / "They appeared to understand the rules." / "The door appeared to be locked."

Pattern 3: It appears + that + sentence
This is a very common pattern in formal English.
"It appears that the file has been deleted." / "It appears that we were wrong."

Pattern 4: appear + in / on / at + place
"She appeared in a film." / "He appeared on the radio." / "They appeared at the summit."

Across all its meanings, "appear" always involves emergence — something or someone coming into awareness:

  • A person appears → comes into sight
  • A person appears tired → tiredness comes through to the observer
  • A person appears in court → they arrive and present themselves
  • A book appears → it comes out into the world
  • A person appears on stage → they come forward in a public role

Once you see this underlying pattern, each meaning of "appear" stops feeling like a separate definition and starts feeling like variations on one clear idea.
